title: What Is Agent Credential Management?
summary: The keys, tokens and secrets agents use to reach enterprise systems: documented lifetimes per credential type, what NIST says a cryptoperiod should be, and why revocation is weaker than assumed.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Agent credential management is not identity plus a vault. It's keeping every credential an agent holds scoped, stored, rotated, and revocable for the agent's entire working life, not just the day it was issued.**


The numbers are in the vendors' own documentation and they do not agree with each other. A GitHub App installation access token expires after one hour. A Google Cloud service account key, by Google's own words, has no expiry time and stays valid until you delete it. A GitHub fine-grained personal access token may be given an infinite lifetime unless an organization policy blocks it. One agent can hold all three.


Most teams get the first half right. They mint a credential and lock it in a vault, and treat that as done. What they miss is the second half: whether that credential is still scoped correctly six months later, whether it rotates on its own, and whether anyone could revoke it in seconds if the agent went rogue.


We are not arguing that vaults are the wrong answer. They are the right answer to storage, and storage is the part almost everyone already solved.


The part to fix this quarter is time. NIST recommends a cryptoperiod of no more than two years for an authorization key, which means that for most enterprises the honest starting question is how old the oldest agent credential in production is, and whether anyone can say.
